title: A hymn in Sarang
hook: Parmanand asks what all your listening has done, and Surdas says whose company to leave

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Sarang, the midday raga, and Guru Nanak calling himself the servant of his own Master. Your line was midday. Did you manage ten seconds with open hands at the busiest point? Day one thousand one hundred seventeen.

What have you done, by listening? That's the question, more or less, that opens today's hymn, and it's a sharp one to hear in a series where every day has asked you to listen. A person sits through the holy stories, hears them told and retold, nods along. Then the hymn asks: and what came of it? It's by the Bhagat Parmanand, one of the voices the Gurus set inside the Sarang section of the Guru Granth Sahib. Near it stands a short verse under the name of Surdas. Today: a hymn in Sarang, and the question it won't let go.
screen: `WHAT HAVE YOU DONE, BY LISTENING?` → `PARMANAND ASKS.` → `SURDAS STANDS NEARBY.`

segments.voice: Here's Parmanand's hymn, in paraphrase. O man, what have you gained from hearing the Puranas told? Steady devotion hasn't welled up in you, and you haven't given to the hungry. Lust hasn't left you, and neither has anger. Greed hasn't let go. You haven't stopped slandering others. Then, in its closing line, the hymn names the company of the holy. Notice what the hymn is aimed at. Not the stories themselves; Parmanand doesn't say a word against them. The target is the listener who hears and stays the same. In the hymn, hearing is supposed to go somewhere: into devotion that holds steady, and into food on a hungry person's plate. If it goes nowhere, the hymn asks what it was for. Surdas's verse makes a matching point from the other side. In paraphrase: O mind, leave the company of those who have turned their backs on the Lord. Parmanand says hearing alone won't change you. Surdas says the people around you will, one way or the other. Put them together and you get a picture of devotion that isn't only an ear. It's hands and feet and the people you sit with. Now set it in Sarang, the midday raga. Midday is lunchtime. It's the hour when a person who has been listening all morning finds out whether any of it reached their hands, whether someone hungry gets fed, whether the slander at the lunch table gets joined or left. That's the line for today. Midday devotion.
screen: `WHAT HAVE YOU GAINED FROM HEARING?` · `NO DEVOTION, NO FOOD FOR THE HUNGRY.` · `SURDAS: LEAVE THAT COMPANY.` · `LISTENING THAT REACHES THE HANDS.` · then, large: `MIDDAY DEVOTION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to one Sarang shabad, then follow it with one thought for your hands. If you can, play Parmanand's hymn or another shabad sung in Sarang. If not, sit in the quiet. Let the breath slow. Ask yourself, without judging, Parmanand's question: of all the good things I've heard lately, what has reached my hands? Let one answer come, even a small one. Then let one more come: one thing your hands could do today, a meal shared, a kind word in place of a sharp one. Just hold it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each slow breath. The bell holds the time.
A hymn in Sarang. Parmanand's question to the person who hears the holy stories and doesn't change, with Surdas's verse beside it about the company you keep. Today's word.
Your line: midday devotion. At lunch today, let one thing you've heard this week turn into something you do: share the food, or leave the gossip. Day one thousand one hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: The Bhagats' hymns in Raga Sarang, Parmanand's among them, are sung in kirtan beside the Gurus' own, and Sikhs join hearing the Word with seva such as serving food in the langar.

notes: Parmanand's hymn is paraphrased (what have you gained from hearing the Puranas; steady devotion hasn't welled up; you haven't given to the hungry; lust, anger, greed not gone; slander not stopped; closing pointer to the company of the holy). The hymn's harsher middle lines are not retold. Please confirm the paraphrase and Ang (1253).
The script says Parmanand 'doesn't say a word against' the stories. Please confirm this reading is fair to the hymn.

Surdas: the Granth holds a short verse under his name in Sarang, next to a hymn of Guru Arjan headed with Surdas's name. The script says only 'a short verse under the name of Surdas' and does not count lines. Please confirm the description and Ang.
